title: A Charge You Can Add and Remove

scenes.tts: Your genome holds about 518 genes for protein kinases. Nearly every one of these enzymes runs the same reaction. It takes a phosphate from A T P and fastens it to a protein. Why would cells lean so heavily on one small chemical group? What makes a phosphate a good switch?
scenes.caption: Your genome holds about 518 genes for protein kinases. Nearly every one of these enzymes runs the same reaction. It takes a phosphate from ATP and fastens it to a protein. Why would cells lean so heavily on one small chemical group? What makes a phosphate a good switch?
scenes.visual: A field of identical purple kinase pills counts up to about 518 and one arrow runs from all of them to a single reaction: a phosphate hops from ATP onto a protein. A question mark settles on the phosphate and the question 'a good switch?' fills the foot of the frame.
scenes.narration: Your genome holds about 518 genes for protein kinases. Nearly every one of these enzymes runs the same reaction. It takes a phosphate from ATP and fastens it to a protein. Why would cells lean so heavily on one small chemical group? What makes a phosphate a good switch?

scenes.tts: A T P sits at millimolar concentration in the cell, so a kinase never waits for its donor. The kinase takes the end phosphate off A T P, leaving A D P. In animals, it almost always fastens that phosphate to a side chain that ends in a hydroxyl group. That means serine, threonine or tyrosine. Near P H seven, the phosphate carries close to two negative charges, on a spot that had none.
scenes.caption: ATP sits at millimolar concentration in the cell, so a kinase never waits for its donor. The kinase takes the end phosphate off ATP, leaving ADP. In animals, it almost always fastens that phosphate to a side chain that ends in a hydroxyl group. That means serine, threonine or tyrosine. Near pH 7, the phosphate carries close to two negative charges, on a spot that had none.
scenes.visual: ATP chips crowd the left; the kinase takes one and the end phosphate leaves it, which becomes ADP. The phosphate crosses to a marked site on a protein blob. Three residue chips appear, then two orange minus signs settle on the phosphate at a spot that had no charge.

scenes.tts: That charge matters, because a folded protein is held in shape by charges that attract and repel each other. Few changes this small disturb it this much. Every copy of a protein flickers among several arrangements, some working and some not. A phosphate makes the arrangements that suit its charge cheaper to occupy, so more copies sit in them. In glycogen phosphorylase, that shifts the enzyme toward its active form, yet the same trick inhibits glycogen synthase.
scenes.visual: The protein from the last scene grows to fill the frame, small plus and minus marks appear inside it and the new charge makes it jolt open. It becomes a pool of eight copies flickering between closed and open. Phosphates land on every copy and most copies settle open. Labelled glycogen phosphorylase, the open copies glow green as the active form; relabelled glycogen synthase, the same open copies turn red as inhibited.

scenes.tts: A phosphatase takes the phosphate off again, with water, and leaves the protein exactly as it was. It does not run the kinase reaction backwards. It runs a different reaction, and each one goes downhill. Think of a whiteboard, where the marker and the eraser are different tools. The cell likewise regulates adding and removing independently, at the price of one A T P per round trip.

scenes.visual: A protein copy wearing a phosphate glides along a lower lane to the left; a phosphatase and a water chip take the phosphate off and the copy is bare again. A separate upper lane for the kinase appears; a reversed copy of its arrow is crossed out; both lanes get a downhill slope. Tags 'marker' and 'eraser' appear. The copy goes round the whole loop once, and a single ATP chip is spent.

scenes.tts: Why does a cell need phosphatases at all? Think of a sink, with the tap running and the drain open, where the water level depends on both. In the same way, the fraction of protein carrying a phosphate depends on both enzymes. A signal can raise that level by activating the kinase, or by inhibiting the phosphatase. Cells do both.
scenes.visual: A tank of twelve protein copies with the kinase as the tap above and the phosphatase as the drain below. Phosphates are added and removed all the time while the level gauge holds still. A signal activates the kinase and the gauge rises; a second signal blocks the phosphatase and it rises again.

scenes.tts: A phosphate makes a good switch for four reasons. It adds charge, and it stays until an enzyme removes it. Different enzymes add it and remove it, and A T P keeps the kinase supplied. So keep this rule. A kinase writes the phosphate, a phosphatase erases it, and the balance of the two sets the level.

scenes.visual: The tank from the last scene returns at rest. Each reason lights its own part: the charge on a phosphate, the phosphate staying on its copy, the kinase and the phosphatase in turn, ATP flowing into the kinase. Everything else dims, and the kinase is tagged writes, the phosphatase erases, and the gauge is tagged level.
